Life in the desert

groups.instruction:
Questions 31-35

Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-G, below.

Questions 36-40

Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?

In boxes 36-40 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.explanation: Answer: FALSE Paragraph 1 states: 'It is the smallest of the four species of oryx'. The statement says it is larger than the others, which contradicts the passage.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 3 says oryx 'can breed at any time of the year '. Births are more frequent after good rains, but they are not limited to one season, so the statement contradicts the passage.

Answer: FALSE Paragraph 3: 'Raising the young is entirely the responsibility of the mother , who guards the calf ... adult males are not involved .' This directly contradicts the idea that males protect calves.

Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 5 mentions that 'domestic goats and camels competed with the oryx for scarce grazing', but the writer treats them together and never compares which animal caused more problems.

Answer: TRUE Paragraph 6: the herd was sent to Phoenix, 'where the hot, dry climate was similar to that of the animals' natural habitat'. A second reason (low disease risk) is also given, so 'partly because the climate was suitable' agrees with the passage.

Answer: TRUE Paragraph 10: 'Governments across the region cooperated closely, exchanging animals to ensure that the herds had as much genetic variety as possible.' 'Shared' paraphrases 'exchanging' and 'genetic diversity' paraphrases 'genetic variety'.
Answer: melons Paragraph 2: 'They feed mainly on grasses, but their diet also includes herbs, roots and wild melons .' Only one word is allowed, so the answer is 'melons'.
Answer: dew Paragraph 2: an oryx gets moisture 'from its food and from the dew that forms on plants overnight'. 'At night' paraphrases 'overnight'.
Answer: skin Paragraph 4: 'its meat was eaten, its skin was turned into leather'. 'Made into leather' paraphrases 'turned into leather'.

Answer: roads Paragraph 5: 'the search for oil brought roads , vehicles and large numbers of workers into parts of the desert that had previously been almost impossible to reach'. Vehicles and workers are not things that are 'built', so only 'roads' fits the note.
Answer: 1972 Paragraph 7: 'In 1972 , the last known wild oryx were shot by a hunting party in central Oman'. Do not confuse this with 1962, the year of Operation Oryx.

Answer: rangers Paragraph 8: 'Members of the local Harasis tribe ... were employed as rangers to follow the herds and record their movements.' 'Monitor the herds' paraphrases 'follow the herds and record their movements'.
Answer: communities Paragraph 11: one of the current goals is 'to maintain the support of local communities '. 'Keep' paraphrases 'maintain'.
Answer: C Section C mentions the few large trees that survived and says 'there are too few of them to draw reliable conclusions '. This is the research difficulty caused by their small number.

Answer: G In section G, Ortiz says 'the benefits are clear' and there is 'a strong reason to go ahead', while Keane is 'less certain' and worries that the new trees are 'not quite the chestnut we lost'. This is a disagreement about planting the new trees.
Answer: B Section B: the fungus 'was accidentally brought into the country in the late 1800s on chestnut trees imported from Asia '.
Answer: E Section E describes a grove in the Midwest, where ' the distance from the eastern forests protected them – there was simply no source of infection nearby'.

Answer: C Section C: 'by the time a stem has reached a few centimetres in diameter , the fungus has found its way in'. This gives the size at which young shoots become infected. (Section F mentions young plants, but only in the context of deliberate testing.)

Answer: B (Samuel Ortiz) Section F: Ortiz says 'You don't have to wait long for an answer ... Within a few months, the susceptible trees have large, swollen cankers '. 'A tree that cannot resist' paraphrases 'susceptible trees'.

Answer: A (Laura Keane) Section G: Keane's organisation ' prefers to focus on protecting and monitoring the wild shoots that are still growing', and she says 'If we give those survivors time and space, some ... may develop a tolerance of their own'.
Answer: B (Samuel Ortiz) Section C: Ortiz says ' It can't simply be chance that these trees are still standing ... we need to find out what's different about them.'
Answer: C (Nora Blake) Section E: Blake says distance protected the grove for decades, but warns ' The blight is already in the next county ... one infected tree is all it would take'.
Answer: A (Laura Keane) Section A: Keane says 'Unless you've seen the old photographs , it's hard to understand what was lost' and describes trunks so wide that three men couldn't reach around them.
Answer: rot Section D: 'above all it resisted rot , so it was widely used for fence posts, telegraph poles and railway sleepers'. 'Not easily affected by' paraphrases 'resisted'.
Answer: leather Section D: the bark and wood were a source of tannin, 'a substance used to turn animal hides into leather '.

Answer: pigs Section D: the nuts were 'fed to the pigs that farmers allowed to roam in the woods'. 'Let wander' paraphrases 'allowed to roam'. Deer, bears, turkeys and squirrels also ate them, but they were wild animals, not animals that were fed by farmers.

text.en: explaining the meaning of a scientific term.
challenging a popular belief about sleep.
pointing out a situation that affects many people.
describing the jobs in which people are most often tired.

questions.explanation: Answer: C The writer opens with ' Many of the choices that shape our lives are made when we are short of sleep ' and gives everyday examples (doctors, new parents, drivers). This points out a common situation. The jobs are only examples, not a list of the most tiring jobs (D), and the writer accepts rather than challenges the belief that tiredness slows us down (B).

text.en: Their changing work patterns made them particularly suitable for the study.
Their ways of coping with tiredness were of special interest to the researchers.
Their long working hours are typical of many healthcare professions.
Their experience of making difficult decisions made them ideal participants.

questions.explanation: Answer: A The nurses work on rotating schedules, and ' because the same people regularly move between being well rested and seriously short of sleep, they allowed us to compare each person with themselves '. Their changing work patterns are what made them suitable. The paragraph does not discuss their coping methods (B), other professions (C) or their decision-making experience (D).

text.en: stating the aims of the research
describing how the study was carried out

questions.explanation: Answer: D The paragraph begins ' This is how we reached that conclusion ' and then explains the procedure: when the nurses were tested, the games they played, the choices offered and how they were paid. This describes the method. The results were given in the previous paragraph (A).

text.en: allow tired people to make decisions more quickly.
help people to recognise when they are too tired to decide.
make potential rewards seem more attractive than usual.
only occur when people are aware that they are taking a risk.

questions.explanation: Answer: C After a sleepless night, ' a region deep inside the brain which responds to rewards became more active when a large win was possible', while the area that encourages caution became less active. This makes rewards more attractive. Speed of decisions (A), self-awareness (B) and conscious risk (D) are not mentioned.

Answer: B Paragraph 5: rested people ' generally take the safe option . That is exactly what we saw after the nurses' day shifts.' 'The option with a guaranteed result' paraphrases 'the safe option' (the guaranteed small sum).
Answer: G Paragraph 5: after night shifts, 'The nurses chose the gamble far more often, particularly when the potential prize was large .'

Answer: F Paragraph 5: 'their willingness to gamble had little connection with how tired they said they felt ; some of those who reported feeling perfectly alert were among the biggest risk-takers.' Their own reports did not reliably show their risk-taking.
Answer: E Paragraph 6: the student volunteers ' stayed awake in our laboratory for an entire night, under supervision ' before playing the games, and their choices then matched the tired nurses'.

Answer: D In both studies, participants were tested after being deprived of sleep (night shifts in the hospital, a sleepless night in the laboratory), and in both cases their choices shifted. D is also the only ending that fits the sentence grammatically, as a noun phrase.
Answer: YES Paragraph 9: when entire teams are short of sleep, ' nobody in the room is in a good position to question a risky plan '. 'Challenge a risky proposal' paraphrases 'question a risky plan'.

Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 10 only discusses phones: people 'keep their phones beside the bed and ... check them if they wake in the night'. Laptops are never mentioned, so no comparison is possible.

Answer: NO Paragraph 11: ' It would be far too simple to claim that tiredness was responsible for the financial crises of recent decades.' The writer rejects this claim. Tiredness may have contributed, but the writer does not see it as the main cause.

Answer: YES Paragraph 11: tired decision-makers were 'focusing on possible profits while paying too little attention to the dangers '. The same idea appears in paragraph 3 ('less concerned about what they might lose').
Answer: YES The final sentence: ' Understanding how tiredness affects our judgement is the first step towards making wiser choices. ' The writer also suggests practical rules based on this knowledge.
